scenes.tts: A neuron can receive an inhibitory input that moves its membrane potential by zero millivolts. It can still stop the cell from firing. How? The usual picture says inputs are voltages that add and subtract. That picture cannot explain this one.
scenes.caption: A neuron can receive an inhibitory input that moves its membrane potential by 0 mV. It can still stop the cell from firing. How? The usual picture says inputs are voltages that add and subtract. That picture cannot explain this one.
scenes.visual: A drawn neuron with a red inhibitory input and a green excitatory input beside a voltage gauge; the dot does not move under inhibition and a boxed question mark sits where the spike should be.
scenes.narration: A neuron can receive an inhibitory input that moves its membrane potential by 0 mV. It can still stop the cell from firing. How? The usual picture says inputs are voltages that add and subtract. That picture cannot explain this one.

scenes.tts: Think of each input as a conductance instead. When a synapse opens channels, it adds conductance, measured in nanosiemens. Those channels have a reversal potential, the voltage at which current through them is zero. Every open conductance pulls the membrane toward its own reversal potential.

scenes.visual: Three channel cards (leak, excitatory, inhibitory) appear with their reversal potentials marked on the gauge; arrows from the voltage dot toward each marker, thicker for larger conductance.
scenes.narration: Think of each input as a conductance instead. When a synapse opens channels, it adds conductance, measured in nanosiemens. scenes.tts: Here is a made up cell, with the same voltage everywhere. All values are illustrative. At rest, the leak conductance is ten nanosiemens, reversing at minus sixty five millivolts. Threshold is minus fifty. Now open an excitatory conductance of five nanosiemens, reversing at zero. The voltage settles at minus forty three point three millivolts. The voltage is an average of the reversal potentials, weighted by conductance. That is above threshold.
scenes.caption: Here is a made-up cell, with the same voltage everywhere. All values are illustrative. At rest, the leak conductance is 10 nS, reversing at −65 mV. Threshold is −50. Now open an excitatory conductance of 5 nS, reversing at 0. The voltage settles at −43.3 mV. The voltage is an average of the reversal potentials, weighted by conductance. That is above threshold.
scenes.visual: Leak alone holds the dot at -65; the excitatory card opens and the dot rises to -43.3 above the threshold line.
scenes.narration: Here is a made-up cell, with the same voltage everywhere. All values are illustrative. At rest, the leak conductance is 10 nS, reversing at −65 mV. Threshold is −50. Now open an excitatory conductance of 5 nS, reversing at 0. The voltage settles at −43.3 mV. The voltage is an average of the reversal potentials, weighted by conductance. That is above threshold.

scenes.tts: Now add an inhibitory conductance of ten nanosiemens. Its reversal potential equals rest. The average now includes a second pull toward rest. The voltage settles at minus fifty two millivolts. That is below threshold, so there is no spike. Take the excitation away, and the inhibition alone leaves the voltage at minus sixty five. The trace does not move, yet it vetoed the spike.
scenes.caption: Now add an inhibitory conductance of 10 nS. Its reversal potential equals rest. The average now includes a second pull toward rest. The voltage settles at −52 mV. That is below threshold, so there is no spike. Take the excitation away, and the inhibition alone leaves the voltage at −65. The trace does not move, yet it vetoed the spike.
scenes.visual: The red card opens at -65; the dot drops from -43.3 to -52, under threshold. Excitation closes and the dot sits at -65 with the red card still open.
scenes.narration: Now add an inhibitory conductance of 10 nS. Its reversal potential equals rest. The average now includes a second pull toward rest. The voltage settles at −52 mV. That is below threshold, so there is no spike. Take the excitation away, and the inhibition alone leaves the voltage at −65. The trace does not move, yet it vetoed the spike.

scenes.tts: Inhibition like this is called shunting. It lowers the input resistance, so the same excitatory current makes a smaller voltage change. It also shortens the time constant, from twenty milliseconds to ten. Give the cell two brief pulses, ten milliseconds apart, each worth two millivolts. Without the shunt, they add up to three point two one millivolts. With the shunt, only two point seven four. The shunt did not shrink each jump. It left less of the first pulse for the second to ride on.
scenes.caption: Inhibition like this is called shunting. It lowers the input resistance, so the same excitatory current makes a smaller voltage change. It also shortens the time constant, from 20 ms to 10 ms. Give the cell two brief pulses, 10 ms apart, each worth 2 mV. Without the shunt, they add up to 3.21 mV. With the shunt, only 2.74. The shunt did not shrink each jump. It left less of the first pulse for the second to ride on.
scenes.visual: A plot computed from the worked problem, labelled in this sketch: two pulses at 0 and 10 ms; yellow trace with time constant 20 ms peaks at 3.21 mV after the second pulse, red trace with 10 ms peaks at 2.74 mV.

scenes.tts: So an inhibitory input is defined by what it does to firing, not by which way the trace moves. Inputs add as conductances. Each one pulls the voltage toward its own reversal potential. A shunt can leave the voltage alone and still veto the spike.
